title: Europe's century of catastrophe need not have happened
gist: Reviewing Rajiv Joseph's play 'Archduke' at London's Royal Court, historian Brendan Simms argues the assassination of Franz Ferdinand and Europe's cascade into war were contingent rather than inevitable — 1913 was trending positively on slavery, parliamentary government and averted crises — and corrects the play's claim that Apis radicalised the Sarajevo conspirators, who had decided to kill the Archduke of their own volition.

insights.claim: In 1913 the world appeared to be trending positively even in retrospect — chattel slavery on the way out, parliamentary government increasing especially in Germany, and wider war already averted over Morocco in 1906 and 1911, the 1908 Bosnia-Herzegovina annexation and the 1912-13 Balkans crises.
insights.speaker: Brendan Simms
insights.so_what: A run of successfully de-escalated crises is not evidence of structural stability — the base rate of averted war says nothing about the next one.
insights.quote: the world appeared to be going in the right direction, with chattel slavery on the way out, parliamentary government on the increase, especially in Germany, and a wider war so far averted over Morocco (1906 and 1911)
insights.locator: I have always dreamed of being transported back to 1913

insights.claim: The First World War, George Kennan's 'great seminal catastrophe' of the century, killed more than fifteen million soldiers and civilians and led directly to the Russian Revolution and communism, and to the rise of Hitler and the Holocaust.
insights.speaker: Brendan Simms
insights.so_what: The canonical case for how a single low-probability political shock compounds into decades of tail outcomes — the argument against dismissing assassination and succession risk.
insights.quote: It not only killed more than fifteen million soldiers and civilians but led directly to the Russian Revolution and the scourge of communism, to the rise of Hitler and thus the Holocaust, and to many other bad outcomes.
insights.locator: The resulting First World War became

insights.claim: The play's most valuable move is to challenge the notion of inevitability by having the cook Sladjana contradict Apis's teleology that the conspirators' martyrdom is pre-ordained and suggesting they could simply get off the train before or after Sarajevo.
insights.speaker: Brendan Simms
insights.so_what: Teleological narratives about conflict are usually constructed after the fact; assuming inevitability removes the off-ramps that actually exist in real time.
insights.quote: Archduke also challenges the notion of inevitability.
insights.locator: Archduke also challenges the notion of inevitability

insights.claim: The assassination itself remained genuinely contingent right up to the moment: Cabrinovic's bomb bounced off the vehicle and exploded under an escorting car, Grabez was too distracted to detonate his bomb or use his pistol, and Princip only fired because the Archduke's car by unhappy coincidence slowed in front of him.
insights.speaker: Brendan Simms
insights.so_what: Two of three attackers failed and the third succeeded on a traffic accident — a concrete reminder that catastrophic outcomes often turn on operational noise, not design.
insights.locator: History tells us that Trifko Grabez did not

insights.claim: The claim that Apis radicalised the Sarajevo conspirators is misleading: they had decided of their own volition to kill the Archduke, and Apis merely provided the weapons and logistical help.
insights.speaker: Brendan Simms
insights.so_what: Directly rebuts the fashionable 'elites whip up populism' framing of political violence — the causal arrow ran from below, with elites supplying means not motive.
insights.quote: If, as some reviewers claim, this play is about how elites whip up populism, the Sarajevo conspirators are not a particularly good example.
insights.locator: Some of this is misleading, however

insights.claim: The play takes considerable liberties with the historical record, including turning the three bullets fired into Apis by a loyal officer into three slugs from Draga's revolver, so it should not be treated as a reliable record of events.
insights.speaker: Brendan Simms
insights.so_what: Dramatised history shapes public intuitions about causation; knowing where the licence sits is the difference between a useful and a misleading mental model.
insights.quote: The playwright takes considerable liberties with the historical record.

insights.claim: What the play does effectively is convey history not as it 'actually was' but, in Ranke's phrase, 'as it essentially was' — brilliantly communicating the toxic cocktail of paranoid nationalism, over-wrought Orthodox religiosity and machismo in the Serb patriot milieu.
insights.speaker: Brendan Simms
insights.so_what: A useful distinction between factual accuracy and atmospheric accuracy when judging any narrative account of a political environment.
insights.quote: The toxic cocktail of paranoid nationalism, over-wrought Orthodox religiosity and machismo which characterised the Serb patriot milieu is brilliantly communicated.
insights.locator: What the play does very effectively

insights.claim: Apis's charisma, brutality and determination make him the most compelling figure in the play, including his account of the 1903 assassination of the Austrophile Serbian royal couple in which he ate part of the King's lung and sawed off the doomed man's fingers as he clung to a balustrade.
insights.speaker: Brendan Simms
insights.so_what: The 1903 regicide establishes that Serbian political violence had an established, institutionalised precedent well before 1914.

insights.claim: Apis is imagined describing Austria-Hungary as 'A two-headed abomination with German leadership in the west and Hungarian in the east' and as 'A twisted Siamese piglet forever defecating into the mouth of its unfortunate twin', which Simms judges plausible in tone if unverifiable.
insights.speaker: Brendan Simms
insights.so_what: Captures how the multinational empire was perceived by its enemies — dysfunction as a structural feature, not a passing crisis.
insights.quote: ‘A two-headed abomination with German leadership in the west and Hungarian in the east’
insights.locator: I don’t know if Apis ever described Austria-Hungary

insights.claim: The play ends with Gavrilo able to imagine not shooting — asking 'What if I didn't?' and proposing they get off the train, meet women and have children — which reframes the assassin as someone making a choice rather than executing destiny.
insights.speaker: Brendan Simms
insights.so_what: Agency-based readings of political violence produce different policy conclusions than structural ones: deterrence and interdiction matter if actors are choosing.
insights.quote: ‘Maybe the world don’t have to end at all. We can just get off the train… Meet some women. Maybe we survive. Have some children.

insights.claim: Princip died in an Austro-Hungarian prison aged 23 with no offspring, yet Simms concludes we are all in a sense his children because we still live in a world he helped to make.
insights.speaker: Brendan Simms
insights.so_what: The single clearest statement of how much of the present order traces to one contingent act by a marginal individual.
insights.quote: He had no offspring, but we are all, in a sense, his children because we still live in a world he helped to make.
insights.locator: Princip later died in an Austro-Hungarian prison
